prompt.context: Your client is Next Level Gaming (NLG), a start-up in the E-sports and computer gaming industry based in Los Angeles, California. NLG is planning to launch its first game – an online, multiplayer role playing game that is unlike any existing franchise. Being a new player in the industry, NLG's CEO, Bobby Beck, has asked for your help in deciding its business model. The company is considering 3 alternatives: a subscription model where players pay a monthly fee; a retail model where players pay full price at initial purchase; and a free-to-play model where the game is free to play but charges players for in-game merchandise.
prompt.question: How would you advise NLG to proceed with its business model selection?

clarifying_info.q: What is the time frame for this launch?
clarifying_info.a: NLG is looking to launch immediately.
The online gaming industry is dominated by 3 major players who control 35%, 25%, and 20% share respectively. There is a long tail of smaller gaming companies.
Based on preliminary market research, NLG expects the majority of players to be between the ages of 21 to 40.
NLG is planning to launch its game in the US only.

clarifying_info.q: What platforms will the game support?
clarifying_info.a: NLG's game is compatible for both Apple and Windows computers.

clarifying_info.q: What has NLG spent on R&D?
clarifying_info.a: NLG spent $10 million USD to develop its first game.

exhibits.title: Revenue Assumptions by Business Model
exhibits.shows: A table comparing revenue-side assumptions across the three business models (Subscription, Retail, Free-To-Play)

exhibits.title: Cost Structure by Business Model
exhibits.shows: A table comparing per-customer variable costs, customer acquisition costs, and shared fixed costs across the three business models

data.Footnote: Per customer costs in the table are for all customers including non-paying customers. Paying customers incur an additional average variable cost of $10

exhibits.title: Beta Test Survey Results
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing survey responses (scale 1–5, where 5 = most likely) from a beta test (n=100) across four questions, broken out by Subscription, Upfront Purchase, and Free-to-Play groups

framework: Quantify profitability for each of the 3 models: estimate # of players acquired and revenue per player, then subtract fixed and variable costs
Compare profit margins (not just absolute profit) across models
Assess qualitative factors: competitive response, customer acquisition cost, long-term retention, alternate revenue streams
Consider future expansion optionality: new platform (mobile/console), new geography, new game launches, e-sports tournaments

questions.prompt: What factors would you consider to estimate the number of players NLG can target with its first game? How large is this player base in the US?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a bottom-up or top-down market sizing. A reasonable approach: US population ~330M, ~25% aged 21-40 = ~82M, apply a share of gamers (e.g. 50-60% of that age group game regularly on PC) giving ~40-50M PC gamers, then apply a share likely to be interested in a new RPG. Target answer should be approximately 10M addressable players. If estimate differs significantly from 10M, the interviewer should guide the candidate to pressure-test assumptions.

math.setup: US population approach to arrive at addressable PC RPG gamers aged 21-40
steps: ~20-25% would be interested in a new online multiplayer RPG = ~8-12M
Round to ~10M as the addressable market

questions.prompt: What is NLG's expected first-year profitability with each of the 3 pricing models?
questions.guidance: Candidate must correctly calculate revenues and total costs for each model. Key trap: the footnote in Exhibit 2 states that per-customer costs apply to ALL customers (including non-paying in F2P), and paying customers incur an additional $10 variable cost. Candidate should also calculate profit margins. Subscription and Free-to-Play have equal absolute profit ($20M) but different margins (16.67% vs 13.33%). Strong candidates note this distinction.

math.setup: Revenue = addressable market * market share * price per player. Costs = (market * share * variable cost per player) + (paying players * additional variable cost if F2P) + fixed costs. Fixed costs total: $5M product dev + $7M server + $3M other = $15M total fixed
math.answer: Subscription: $20M profit (16.67% margin); Retail: $9M profit (12.50% margin); Free-to-Play: $20M profit (13.33% margin)

questions.prompt: How does the beta test survey data impact your outlook on the 3 different business models?
questions.guidance: Candidate should interpret Exhibit 3 systematically. Key insights: (1) Retail/Upfront Purchase shows low loyalty and low add-on intent - poor long-term model. (2) Subscription and Free-to-Play both show high retention intent (~4.2 and ~4.1). (3) Free-to-Play scores highest on recommending to friends (4.8 vs 1.2/1.8) - strong viral growth potential. (4) Subscription users are more likely to switch to a competing game (3.6) vs Free-to-Play (1.9) - Free-to-Play has stickier base. (5) A higher score on 'Switch to new game' is unfavorable. Note: n=100 is statistically significant for a beta test context.

math.setup: No calculation required; qualitative interpretation of bar chart values
steps: Continue playing after year 1: Sub 4.2, Retail 1.2, F2P 4.1 — Retail players drop off; Sub and F2P are sticky
Purchase add-ons: Sub 4.0, Retail 1.5, F2P 2.3 — Sub players most willing to buy add-ons
Recommend to friends: Sub 1.2, Retail 1.8, F2P 4.8 — F2P has strongest viral potential
Switch to competing game: Sub 3.6, Retail 4.2, F2P 1.9 — F2P most resilient to competition (lower = better here)
math.answer: Retail model has poor retention and loyalty. F2P has highest viral growth and competitive resilience. Sub has strong retention and add-on revenue potential but is more vulnerable to competitor switching.

brainstorming.prompt: What non-financial factors would you consider in choosing between the subscription vs. free-to-play business models?

categories.name: Competitive Response
ideas: If a competitor launches a game in the same genre, how sticky is NLG's player base?
Free-to-play's lower switching cost (survey score 1.9 vs sub 3.6) suggests stronger resilience
Subscription model risks churn if a competing title launches at a lower price or free

categories.name: Growth Potential
ideas: New platform: expand from PC to mobile or console to reach broader audience
New geography: expand outside the US to capture global gaming markets
New game: launch a 2nd-generation game to retain existing players and create new content
E-sports: hosting tournaments contingent on building a sufficiently large player base

categories.name: Alternate Revenue Streams
ideas: Merchandising: branded merchandise for loyal players
In-game sponsorships or advertising for the free-to-play model
E-sports prize pools and sponsorship deals once player base is large enough

categories.name: Consumer Preference & Trends
ideas: Risk that more players migrate to mobile platforms over time, affecting PC-centric revenue
Generational shift: new cohorts of gamers may prefer different genres or formats
Free-to-play is the dominant model globally for online multiplayer games, aligning with consumer trend

categories.name: Customer Acquisition & Retention
ideas: Free-to-play has the lowest CAC ($7 vs $35 sub, $18 retail) enabling faster player base growth
Subscription requires ongoing value justification to retain monthly payers
Free-to-play benefits from network effects: larger player base improves game quality and community

recommendation: Recommend the free-to-play business model for NLG's launch
Free-to-play captures the largest player base (50% market share vs 10-12%), maximizing network effects and competitive resilience
Absolute first-year profit is equal to subscription ($20M) but with a significantly larger installed base to monetize going forward
Beta test data confirms F2P players have highest intent to recommend (4.8) and lowest intent to switch to a competitor (1.9), indicating a sticky and viral player base
The lower variable cost per user ($13+$7=$20 vs sub $85) provides operational leverage as the player base scales
risks: Key risk: generating a sufficient percentage of paying players (currently projected at 30%) — if this drops, revenue falls sharply
Risk of in-game purchase fatigue: players may resist paying if purchases feel pay-to-win rather than cosmetic
Subscription model may generate more predictable, recurring cash flows which F2P lacks
next_steps: Design two in-game purchase tiers: cosmetic (character aesthetics) and progression (expedite leveling) to maximize paying conversion across different player segments
Conduct deeper analysis on the 30% paying player assumption; A/B test pricing of in-game items during soft launch
Evaluate expansion roadmap: mobile platform first (largest addressable market), then international geographies
Monitor player lifetime value vs customer acquisition cost quarterly to ensure F2P unit economics remain favorable
Explore e-sports tournament hosting once player base crosses a critical mass threshold
